title: The Philidor Defense
subtitle: The rook ending every defender must know.
goals: Switch to rear checks at the right moment
Choose the short side for your king

steps.say: The Philidor position — the defensive twin of the Lucena, published in 1777. You're a pawn down in a rook ending, but your king sits on the queening square. Defended correctly, this is a DEAD DRAW — and the method is so precise it feels like a magic spell. Learn it once, save half-points forever.

steps.prompt: You're BLACK, defending. Philidor's immortal rule: put your rook on the THIRD rank (your sixth) — the fence!
hints: White wins only if his KING reaches the sixth rank. Deny every one of those squares at once.
Ra6! The rook patrols the sixth rank like an electric fence — the white king can never cross.

line.say: The Philidor fence! White's king may never step to d6, e6 or f6 — and without the king, the pawn cannot advance safely. White can shuffle forever; you just sweep the rook along the sixth.

rejections.say: You checked him FORWARD — Kd6! and suddenly mate threats loom around your king. Checks come LATER; first build the fence on the sixth: Ra6.
Passive shuffling lets Kd6 in with menace. The DRAW lives on the sixth rank — Ra6, the fence Philidor taught in 1777.

steps.wrongSay: Deny the white king the entire sixth rank with one rook move.
steps.successSay: Fence on the sixth: White's king is locked out and the position cannot be lost.

steps.prompt: White got impatient and pushed the pawn to the sixth. Philidor's second command: NOW the rook dives — checks from behind, forever!
hints: The pawn on e6 is a wall now — White's own king can never hide from checks BEHIND it. The fence has done its job.
Send the rook to the first rank: Ra1! The checks from the rear can never be escaped.

line.say: The dive! Now Rf1+, Re1+, endless — the white king has no shelter anywhere: his own pawn blocks the only hiding square. This exact two-step (fence, then dive the moment the pawn advances) is the whole Philidor draw.

rejections.say: Kxe6!! You traded your entire rook for one pawn — now White's rook mates your bare king at leisure. The pawn wasn't the enemy; the KING crossing was. Dive behind: Ra1.
Too passive — White's king walks in and the mating nets appear. The moment the pawn touched the sixth rank, your rook's job changed: infinite checks from BEHIND. Ra1!

steps.wrongSay: The advanced pawn now blocks its own king's shelter. Get the rook maximum distance behind for endless checks.
steps.successSay: Fence until the pawn advances, then dive and check forever. Philidor's recipe — unbeatable for 250 years.

steps.prompt: White's rook checks you off the queening square. Grandmaster precision: which way does your king step?
hints: Rule: the defending king goes to the SHORT side of the pawn (fewer files), so your rook keeps the LONG side for checking distance.
For an e-pawn the short side is the kingside — Kf7! — leaving the whole queenside as your rook's runway.

line.say: Short side! Your king huddles in the small corner while your rook owns the long a-file runway — Ra2, Ra5+, endless sideways checks with room to spare. King short, rook long: the mantra of every rook-ending defender.

rejections.say: The LONG side — now your own king stands in your rook's checking lanes, and White's king finds shelter on the wide wing. Defensive geometry says: king to the SHORT side (f7), rook to the long.
Staying in the pawn's path lets White's king muscle forward with tempo. Step aside — to the SHORT side: Kf7 keeps your rook's checking distance intact.

steps.wrongSay: Count the files on each side of the e-pawn: three on one side, four on the other. Your king takes the SMALL side.
steps.successSay: Fence, dive, short side — the complete defensive toolkit for rook endings. You now hold draws that club players lose every day.
